summary.text: Take \(n=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009=33085221781504\). Using \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\) and multiplicativity over these coprime prime-power factors gives \(\sigma(n)=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=132367152569399\), hence \(a(n)=1\), although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\operatorname{def}(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
and hence
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit the positive integer
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009=33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504
\]
for which \(a(N)=1\). Since this integer is neither \(1\) nor \(12\), it disproves the proposed characterization.

We first record and justify the primality information used in the calculation. The numbers \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. Here is a concise primality check, included so that the factorization of \(N\) is fully justified.

We use the following elementary order criterion. Suppose that the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and that there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv 1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(m-1)/q}-1,m\bigr)=1.
\]
Then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(m\), and let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\). The first congruence shows that \(t\mid m-1\). For each prime power \(q^e\) occurring in \(m-1\), the gcd condition implies that \(b^{(m-1)/q}\not\equiv1\pmod r\), so \(t\nmid(m-1)/q\). Consequently the full power \(q^e\) divides \(t\). This holds for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(m-1\), and therefore \(m-1\mid t\). Thus \(t=m-1\). On the other hand, the order of a nonzero residue modulo the prime \(r\) divides \(r-1\), so \(m-1\mid r-1\). Hence \(r\ge m\). Since \(r\mid m\), also \(r\le m\), and therefore \(r=m\); thus \(m\) itself is prime.

The small numbers \(19\), \(29\), and \(229\) are prime by trial division. For \(19\) and \(29\), one need only test the primes at most their square roots. For \(229\), the primes at most \(\sqrt{229}<16\) are \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), and none divides \(229\): its remainders modulo these primes are respectively \(1,1,4,5,9,8\).

Next,
\[
57251-1=57250=2\cdot 5^3\cdot229.
\]
Repeated squaring gives the following congruences modulo \(57251\):
\[
2^{57250}\equiv1,
\qquad 2^{28625}\equiv57250,
\qquad 2^{11450}\equiv55371,
\qquad 2^{250}\equiv48088.
\]
The last three exponents are \(57250/2\), \(57250/5\), and \(57250/229\), respectively. Euclid's algorithm gives
\[
\gcd(57250-1,57251)=\gcd(57249,57251)=1,
\]
\[
\gcd(55371-1,57251)=\gcd(55370,57251)=1,
\]
and
\[
\gcd(48088-1,57251)=\gcd(48087,57251)=1.
\]
The order criterion therefore proves that \(57251\) is prime.

Now
\[
4409-1=4408=2^3\cdot19\cdot29.
\]
Again by repeated squaring, this time modulo \(4409\),
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1,
\qquad 3^{2204}\equiv4408,
\qquad 3^{232}\equiv209,
\qquad 3^{152}\equiv3965.
\]
Here \(2204=4408/2\), \(232=4408/19\), and \(152=4408/29\). The corresponding gcds are
\[
\gcd(4408-1,4409)=\gcd(4407,4409)=1,
\]
\[
\gcd(209-1,4409)=\gcd(208,4409)=1,
\]
and
\[
\gcd(3965-1,4409)=\gcd(3964,4409)=1.
\]
The criterion proves that \(4409\) is prime.

Finally,
\[
458009-1=458008=2^3\cdot57251.
\]
Modulo \(458009\), repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{458008}\equiv1,
\qquad 3^{229004}\equiv458008,
\qquad 3^8\equiv6561.
\]
The latter two exponents are \(458008/2\) and \(458008/57251\). Moreover,
\[
\gcd(458008-1,458009)=\gcd(458007,458009)=1
\]
and
\[
\gcd(6561-1,458009)=\gcd(6560,458009)=1.
\]
The criterion therefore proves that \(458009\) is prime as well. Thus \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are powers of three distinct primes and are pairwise coprime.

We now reduce the calculation of \(a(n)\) to two standard multiplicative divisor sums. Define
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Then, directly from the definition of \(a(n)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr)\\
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-S(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

Both \(\sigma\) and \(S\) are multiplicative. To see the first assertion, if \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime, every divisor of \(uv\) is uniquely of the form \(xy\), where \(x\mid u\) and \(y\mid v\); consequently
\[
\sigma(uv)=\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}xy
 =\left(\sum_{x\mid u}x\right)\left(\sum_{y\mid v}y\right)
 =\sigma(u)\sigma(v).
\]
Using the same unique representation of divisors and the just-proved multiplicativity of \(\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(uv)
 &=\sum_{d\mid uv}\sigma(d)
 =\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}\sigma(xy)\\
 &=\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}\sigma(x)\sigma(y)
 =S(u)S(v).
\end{aligned}
\]

For a prime \(p\),
\[
\sigma(p^k)=1+p+\cdots+p^k.
\]
In particular,
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15}\right)-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime \(p\) occurring to the first power,
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1
\]
and
\[
S(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sigma(4409)=4410,\qquad S(4409)=4411,
\]
and
\[
\sigma(458009)=458010,\qquad S(458009)=458011.
\]

Applying multiplicativity to the pairwise coprime factors of \(N\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=\sigma(2^{14})\sigma(4409)\sigma(458009)\\
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two factors multiply to
\[
32767\cdot4410=144{,}502{,}470,
\]
and hence
\[
\sigma(N)=144{,}502{,}470\cdot458010
=66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700.
\]
Likewise,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
 &=S(2^{14})S(4409)S(458009)\\
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here
\[
65519\cdot4411=289{,}004{,}309,
\]
so
\[
S(N)=289{,}004{,}309\cdot458011
=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399.
\]
Substitution into \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-S(n)\) now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\cdot66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, the value of the counterexample itself follows from
\[
4409\cdot458009=2{,}019{,}361{,}681
\]
and \(2^{14}=16384\), giving
\[
N=16384\cdot2{,}019{,}361{,}681
 =33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504.
\]
This is plainly neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus the statement that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) holds if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\), fails at \(n=N\). Hence the conjecture is false.
